newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU 1997 budget enters last lap of negotiations.
newsitem.headline: EU 1997 budget enters last lap of negotiations.

text.p: The EU's 1997 draft budget, an unprecedented attempt at freezing spending, will be taken up by the European Parliament in October before final consideration by both the EP and the Council later in the year.

This annual ritual, where Parliament and the Council play financial ping-pong with various spending items -- the Council's non-obligatory spending cuts are typically reinstated by the Parliament -- is more important than usual given the strain governments are under in curbing their own deficits.
Any savings realised in the EU's 1997 budget will be returned to national governments and ease the process of bringing deficits in line with the Maastrict treaty's criteria.
The sums involved could be enormous.
It is estimated that roughly 9.0 billion Ecus will be returned to governments this year from savings in 1995.

Because of persistent underspending in both the agricultural and structural funds sectors, the Council in July proposed a draft budget for next year which slashes 2.5 billion Ecus -- 1.0 billion each in agriculture and structural funds and a further 500 million out of internal and external policies.
Most expect the Parliament to reinstate some of the Council's cuts. As one EU budget official put it: "Of course the Parliament will react to the Council's cuts by their own means."
But since the Parliament has budgetary authority only over non-obligatory spending items -- everything outside of agriculture, which eats up much of the budget -- its influence is limited.

EU officials caution, however, that the amount the EU actually spends on agriculture in 1997 could be substantially altered by two factors: prices for farm products on the world market and the mad cow crisis.
"It's very difficult to estimate what will be needed in the latter of 1997 because of the world market and BSE," said an official.
In the structural funds area, Spain, Greece, Portugal and Ireland, the primary recepients of such aid, were spared any harm under the Council's first draft in July.
Where the Parliament is likely to flex its muscle, therefore, is on spending in internal and external policies.
The Parliament is expected to take up the draft budget in the week of October 21.
The Council's second reading takes place on November 19, after which the budget goes back to the Parliament for a final reading on December 12.
